CUT/SEW Interview

August 31, 2026 by Mandy
Tags: article, cut/sew, interview, madison may, otakon
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 17:29
Instaread

Do you want to start sewing, but feel too intimidated or don’t know where to start? Enter CUT/SEW Patternmaking Studios, offering beginner friendly sewing patterns for cosplay and street fashion, made independently in the USA.

CUT/SEW ran the Cosplay Studio workshops and Crafter Party at Otakon 2026. We got to chat with owner and founder Madison May to learn more about the business and programming. Read til the end for her advice for cosplayers and crafters!

Tell us about the history of Cut & Sew Studios.

Madison: “We are a super small indie brand and private studio. Currently we only have two people full-time, and the rest are contractors. We were crowdfunded through Indiegogo. I was working in professional costuming at a shop that was doing a lot of work for cruises, theme parks, and television. And it was just a very stressful experience. I was an active cosplayer at the time. I don’t really have time to do it that much anymore, unfortunately.

But I had a bunch of friends that were really active in the community and somebody had said: ‘Hey, it’s really hard to get patterns for this niche and to find things that aren’t just Simplicity [patterns]. Why don’t you start a pattern making company?’ Because I was patterning at the shop at the time. So that’s kind of where everything started and it grew very, very slowly from there. That was ten years ago; this year is our 10th anniversary, which is crazy. We’re still growing. We’re still very small. I’m hoping to change that soon enough. We’re very artist and community driven; that’s kind of the path forward.”

For the programming that you do at conventions, I saw you had a booth at the dealers room where you have patterns and supplies for sale, plus the workshops. What kind of workshops do you offer, and could you speak to why you choose those topics?

“It’s kind of like half logistical, half need for the area. The Cosplay Studio hosts a series of workshops that we run all around the country. We’ve gotten so much feedback that it’s [crafting] just really hard to learn, particularly with JoAnn’s being gone, and also just in general. And the beginner-friendly and learning aspect of making is so integral to what we do that I really wanted to find a way to offer that in a place where cosplayers/makers already were and where we could have our own time. There are people all over the country who need access to these kinds of educational opportunities. 

The classes that we offer really depend on where we’re at, tailored to the con, attendees, and instructors. We basically approach conventions and ask who will have us and let us do this thing. We ask what they notice in the contests, how can we support the contests, and what types of makers they already have. Then we gather data and go, okay, so this did really well, this didn’t. We also send out surveys at the end to our workshop attendees. We ask what did you like, what did you not like, what do you want to see? That information really guides what we do moving forward. And just talking to people. I’m at the cosplay studio from morning till morning basically because I do the Crafter Party event which goes past midnight, so I really get a lot of time to talk to people and get a first-hand feel for what people are looking for at each individual con.

Otakon is a very tech-heavy space, I would say, and it’s very advanced. Some of our beginner-friendly classes go over very well for sewing, but more advanced classes such as the metal dice casting, 3D print finishing, leather-working, and tambour embroidery sell out really fast.”

How long have you been hosting cosplay workshops?

“A couple of years now. I feel it was a post-pandemic thing for sure. We started because we started a relationship with Famore Cutlery, which is a really, really awesome scissor brand. They’re a really small business as well and they’re super aligned with us in terms of really caring about cosplayers/makers and wanting to help them in the community. They were already doing some workshops and going through a change of management…so we sort of absorbed what they were already doing, refined it, and started pitching it to different places around 2022-2023.

Participants in the leather crafting workshop.

I feel like we finally have our sea legs with it. We have it down pat at this point so we can plead with cons because the feedback we get is overwhelmingly positive. People have such a good time; they feel like they get so much value out of it. I teach a sewing class for beginners and those classes are always so rewarding to me because people come up and say it’s so helpful. It’s so much harder to learn from just tools compared to having somebody in front of you showing you exactly how to do it…being encouraging and making them feel like they can actually tackle sewing, which can be so intimidating.”

Right, getting that hands-on help in the moment rather than through a Youtube video. I haven’t opened up my sewing machine in years because I’m just intimidated by it!

“No yeah, it’s super scary. You know what I find really interesting is that more often than not, the people that come to me aren’t newbies. They have a mission or some experience. They know what they’re doing, but they just feel so intimidated that they give up, you know? I know it’s a challenging craft — so much of crafting is — but I just want to be out there encouraging people to trust themselves. Be willing to make mistakes and just get it done because that’s the only way you learn. So I feel like more than anything, the classes are great and it’s awesome to learn the skill, but even just having the support to have somebody witness that you did it. Like, that’s awesome. You finished it. It’s incredibly important to build that confidence.”

Let’s move on to the Crafter Party. I’ve never heard of a crafting after party event! I know Otakon in particular has a lot of after dark programming, so I want to get a little more insight and how the event came to be, what you do there, and the feedback on that.

“It’s partially it’s they asked us to do something and so we figured out something. Otakon came to us saying they really want more programming in the rooms; they don’t want to shut the rooms down. Our classes usually end around 8:30 PM, so they wanted to add more programming since Otakon is in such high demand. So I was chatting with my team, trying to figure something out, and literally, like a bolt from heaven, the term Crafter Party came to me.

It’s actually really cool because there’s so much high-energy late night programming [at Otakon]. There’s kind of nothing in between panels that’s engaging and active without being kind of manic. For me, I love cons, but sometimes I’m really just too tired to do something like the rave. I want to do something where I could just hang out with my friends because that’s kind of what I’m there to do anyway.”

“We pitched Crafter Party as a way to make new friends because we have these circular shared tables and shared space. You can also hang out with your existing friends, listen to music, and work on crafts. So many people come in with cosplays that they’re crunching on which I find so fun because we have all this equipment too and it just sits there overnight. We open up the rooms and if you need supplies, come up and ask us — we’ll grab it for you. I brought over sewing machines, scissors, pins, specialty glue, specialty products. But if you don’t have something that you’re already working on, you can just hang out, color, and make friendship bracelets. And again, just use the stuff that we have in stock.

Within the Crafter Party, we have the little maker’s market, which we’re still workshopping and trying to get a little bigger because it’s so hard for people to find fabric and supplies. People have a lot of stuff in their stash, so there’s the strong need to destash so that you don’t get overloaded by our craft supplies. We’re really lucky to have storage and studio space. So I was like, let’s just open that up and let people donate things. We can use stuff that we don’t use anymore and have a take what you want space for de-stashing and re-stashing, I guess.”

I love that! I relate to that need to destash, which is why I enjoy events like craft swaps.

“For me personally, so much of what I do in CUT/SEW, just to be totally honest, is the stuff that I wanted when I was younger. I love all the crafting shop stuff, but I’m on the road all the time for cons. I kind of miss stuff that happens in my local community. So we just need to build the community. Like Field of Dreams — if you build it, they will come to you.”

Where do you recommend cosplayers source materials? Do you have any specific websites you recommend or shops you recommend?

“We’re all kind of in this weird in-between period, so I try really hard to share what I know. We’re doing so much work right now behind the scenes to work with distributors in the sewing industry and local craft shops and small businesses to really have them accept and welcome cosplay. 

If you are lucky enough to have a quilt shop or a small sewing shop in your area, I highly, highly, highly recommend starting there. JoAnn’s closing sucked, but it was kind of a necessary evil because getting rid of the big business of sewing is the only way that we’re going to keep the small community of sewing, if that makes sense. Obviously I don’t want anyone to lose access to supplies if they live in an area where they don’t really have a lot of shops, but it does give cosplayers a lot of power to be able to go to their local stores and say ‘Hey, we’re already here. We want XYZ.’ In the background, we’re basically on the ground contacting shops, working for our distributors, showing off how important cosplay is. We have all these educational resources for retailers; we literally have created a whole video course for retailers. We’re just trying to convince them that serving cosplay is really important so they start carrying these products. We’re creating this kind of small sewing ecosystem, which is still in progress.”

Workshop signups, plus examples of the projects.

“If you do not have a store nearby and you just want something online for hardware and sewing supplies, I always recommend Wawak. It’s really great. I used that for years when I was working in the costume industry to stock our costume shops. 

Fabric Wholesale Direct is honestly the one that has the most amount of things, but it’s not always organized super well in terms of the type of material. You have to know what you’re looking for, which is really hard. I think a lot of cosplayers are beginners and so they don’t necessarily know the names of the fabrications, which can be really challenging. Hence why it’s important, I think, more than anything to kind of keep at it with your local stores, because your local stores will serve you, if they know you’re there and they have enough people asking. So I think that’s still going to be the best option in the long term. 

One more thing that I recommend is Creative Reuse, which is a principle in some stores where people are able to come in and drop stuff off that you can shop. There’s a really, really big, great one called Scrap Exchange in Durham, North Carolina. There’s another one called Turnip Green. But I do recommend people use Google to see if they can find something. That’s such a great way to get all of the weird notions and supplies that cosplayers are looking for. It’s going to be a lot harder to find things that are exactly what you’re looking for for a character. I think we’re definitely becoming more and more scrappy as cosplayers.”

What really interested me about CUT/SEW are the patterns. Could you give some insight as to how you come up with concepts for these patterns? Is it based on demand or things that you wish that you had patterns for? How do you determine the designs, and how do they come to fruition?

“I’m the head pattern maker and the designer. The way that I start thinking about what we need and what we don’t want is by going to cons, looking around, and talking to people. This is overwhelmingly a community-based business and so much of what I do is just walk around cons, kind of take notes and see what people are doing, what people need, what people are struggling with. Talking to people [at the dealers booth and workshops] is really great because I get a lot of information and requests as well. Yes, the dealers booth is a sales space, but it’s also a question and answer space. We can give recommendations and one-on-one help, which is so awesome. But it also kind of allows us to see what people are working on.

My job is to pick all the shapes. We try to start with concepts rather than a specific complicated character design. Instead I want to make something that people can really use for any project, because a lot of patterns and sewing comes from the same sort of base shape, just slightly modified. My goal is to provide those shapes in a way where you can convert it to whatever character you’re going to do. Because ultimately, with cosplay, the devil’s in the details. So what we’re trying to do is to provide the main template, and then you can go in with those details to make your specific character.

The Seifuku pattern is a great example. That’s one of our best sellers because there are so many series that have school uniforms, and the only thing you really need to do is change the colors and fabric that you took out. Or maybe the top is slightly longer or the skirt’s slightly longer. But we have the instructions included in the patterns on how to modify to make it that way. Step one is on the ground research at cons, and then step two is simplifying, trying to get a silhouette down to its most basic parts so that it can be used for as many different projects as possible.”

Do you have any general advice for cosplayers and crafters?

“I highly recommend building a community around whatever you’re trying to do. Having a community will help give you the encouragement and reinforcement that you actually can complete a project. It can be very isolating to do it on your own when you’re new, so creating a support network is really, really important. If you don’t have a support network currently, look in your local area for crafting groups or reuse groups or sewing groups. Or just search out cosplayers in your area. Cosplayers are so chill and so friendly; they’re genuinely the nicest people I’ve ever met. They’re always happy to chat and to share their resources.

You have to just do it. Nobody likes that advice but it is very much the most basic approach. You need to make mistakes and get messy. Do a project. Start with something really simple. Everybody always wants to start with really complicated projects. And I love that, but it does make it hard because if you don’t know what you’re doing or if you run into issues, you’re more likely to give up and feel too intimidated. Start working super simple. If you want to learn sewing, start with making a tote bag or start with making a pillow with scraps. [jokingly] Everybody hates the pillow. I chose the pillow in my cosplay for beginners class and we always joke about it because the pillow is such a stupid beginner-friendly thing that if you had a home ec class or Girl Scouts, you learned how to make it. But it is a really great beginner-friendly project to get you familiar with how to use the machine. So make something and be prepared for it to be bad. And that’s okay. It should be bad. It doesn’t matter if it doesn’t look perfect. What matters is that you did it and it’s done. You made something out of nothing, and that is worth celebrating.”

Thank you so much to Madison for her time and insights. Visit cutsew.co to shop their patterns and see where they’re hosting future workshops. Follow them on Instagram and join their Discord for cosplay/sewing tips, tricks, and advice.
